title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model: gpt-5-mini), and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) running the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two preregistration/execution issues affect interpretation: (1) shared-generation semantics removed the per-arm stochasticity assumed by the preregistered power calculation, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable benefit in this executed artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred; results do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, repair budget, or verifier.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) promise automation of intent→configuration translation for network operators but raise operational-safety concerns: stochastic generators can emit syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect command sequences that violate topology-aware invariants (reachability, required workflow sequences, protected interfaces). To mitigate mechanically checkable failure modes, prior work recommends interposing deterministic validators and invoking iterative repair when checks fail—an architecture commonly called generate–verify–repair (GVR) [1,2]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (study c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) to test whether a bounded GVR loop (deterministic verifier + at most one bounded LLM repair attempt) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations relative to an unconstrained LLM baseline (and, prespecified, relative to a schema-constrained baseline). The run used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (240 paired tasks across 12 topology/policy clusters), a single generator/prompt pairing (requested_model = gpt-5-mini), and a deterministic pybatfish-style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applying the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. The registered execution adopted generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Execution and analysis were frozen prior to observing outcomes and the archived artifacts are the authoritative record for all numerical claims.
sections.related_work: Three literature streams ground this study. First, empirical analyses document LLM hallucinations and incorrect outputs for code and structured artifacts, motivating deterministic verification in downstream pipelines because unconstrained generation can produce plausible but incorrect artifacts that fail deeper invariants [9,1]. Second, methodological and systems work on constrained decoding, schema-constrained generation, and generate–verify–repair report measurable improvements on mechanically checkable properties (syntactic validity, compilability, schema compliance) when validators or grammar constraints are interposed between generation and acceptance; these studies motivate GVR architectures but also note that syntactic gains need not imply domain-level semantic correctness for complex NetOps invariants [2,3,8]. Third, NetOps-specific research has developed prototype intent-translation systems and advocates verifier-driven evaluation (reachability and policy invariants) and human oversight for high-stakes changes; integration of LLMs with network verifiers is a recommended pattern in deployment and prototype reports [4,5,6]. Our study differs in being fully preregistered with a frozen analysis executor, using a paired confirmatory design on a synthetic task bank with explicit deterministic verifier predicates, and by executing under shared-initial-candidate semantics that removed within-pair stochastic variation. The literature motivates the experimental question—does bounded GVR reduce verifier-detected semantic violations under realistic generator/verifier trade-offs?—and also highlights the sensitivity of such tests to generation semantics, verifier coverage, and task difficulty [1–6].
sections.methodology: Estimand and design. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed by a frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistration specified two primary contrasts (GVR vs unconstrained baseline; GVR vs schema-constrained decoding) with Bonferroni correction and a fixed-N design (task_count = 240). Execution contract and critical parameters. The adapter_family used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with declared requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Executed parameters of direct relevance to interpretation were: generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (single bounded repair attempt), and retrieval_augmented_generation = false. The deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applying the full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule that checks required command sequences, topology-aware reachability, protected-interface preservation, and final-state predicates; the validator returns structured diagnostics including violation_count and violation lists. Task bank and difficulty metadata. The synthetic task bank contains 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks. Each task encodes an initial device state, a natural-language intent, workflow constraints (required_sequence), and an expected final state; tasks include difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) used by the validator when generating traces. Execution semantics and paired accounting. The preregistered design envisioned independent per-condition generation to create within-pair discordance potential. The archived execution instead used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one generator call per task produced a shared initial candidate reused by both arms; the bounded repair loop executed only if the verifier failed that candidate. Analysis plan. The frozen analysis executor performed an exact McNemar two-sided test on the paired outcomes and computed absolute risk reductions with paired-bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness, contamination, and conservative sensitivity rules were preregistered and are enforced by the executor; no failed episodes or flagged contamination items occurred in this run.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. Planned_episode_count = 480 (two conditions × 240 tasks); completed_episode_count = 480; failed_episode_count = 0; complete_pair_count = 240; model_calls_used = 240 (shared-initial-candidate semantics produced one initial generation per task reused across arms). Every shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier for every task in both arms: contingency counts n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (percentile; 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair usage. For every episode the validator trace records repair_applied = false; the bounded repair loop never executed because the shared initial candidate satisfied all verifier predicates across the full task set. Diagnostic examples. Representative validator traces (archived) show normalized configurations, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation_count = 0 both before and after validation (e.g., a medium-difficulty task with required_command_count = 4 had parsed_command_count = 4, violation_count = 0 and repair_applied = false). Deterministic reconciliation. The reconciled execution manifest confirms provider-call accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, cache_miss_count = 240, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 240}, and all deterministic consistency checks passed.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and statistical degeneracy. The observed outcome is a degenerate paired null: with zero discordant pairs (n_10 + n_01 = 0), there is no within-pair information to estimate a differential effect—the exact McNemar test therefore returns p = 1.00 and the bootstrap procedure yields a point mass CI [0.0, 0.0]. This degeneracy is a direct consequence of the executed generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, which collapsed the per-pair stochasticity assumed by the preregistered power calculation. Scientific implication: within the executed artifact-backed setting (single generator/prompt pairing, shared-initial-candidate semantics, synthetic task bank, single bounded repair attempt, deterministic validator), bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable value because no verifier-detectable errors occurred. This is not evidence that GVR cannot provide value under different semantics: measurable benefit requires (i) generator-produced verifier-detectable failures, (ii) verifier coverage of operationally relevant invariants, and (iii) a repair budget and repair strategy sufficient to correct failures [1–6]. Design lessons for NetOps evaluation. Two evaluation-design choices critically determine ability to detect GVR benefits: (a) generation semantics (shared vs independent) govern discordance potential—if the goal is to measure GVR’s efficacy correcting stochastic generator errors, independent per-condition generation is required; and (b) verifier completeness and adversarial/golden-task selection determine whether the task set produces verifier-detectable failures. The preregistration included golden-reference injections (10% of tasks) and adversarial checks to validate verifier sensitivity; the archived adapter-configured run did not realize the golden-injection step and did not execute the prespecified schema-constrained baseline, which constrains inference. Operational recommendations grounded in the run. To restore the preregistered inferential assumptions and robustly evaluate GVR we recommend: (1) rerunning the frozen task bank with independent_condition_generation = true to restore discordance potential under identical RNG seeds; (2) injecting the prespecified golden/adversarial tasks (10% plan) to validate verifier sensitivity and detect oracle false negatives; (3) expanding generator scope to multi-model regimes to assess cross-model robustness; and (4) increasing the repair budget or allowing iterative repairs to measure multi-iteration convergence properties. Each recommendation follows from the archived execution-accounting and deterministic reconciliation and is framed as evaluation restoration rather than a claim about GVR efficacy. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the executed shared-generation semantics violated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption, eliminating within-pair stochastic variation. Construct validity: passing the deterministic validator does not guarantee absence of operational risks outside the validator’s encoded invariants (oracle incompleteness risk). External validity: synthetic tasks, a single model (gpt-5-mini), and a single repair budget limit generalization. Conclusion validity: zero discordant outcomes preclude evidence that bounded GVR changes verifier-detectable rates under the executed semantics. Relation to prior work. Our artifact-backed null is consistent with the literature’s emphasis that measured GVR gains depend on the baseline generator error rate and verifier coverage: GVR improves mechanically checkable properties when generator failures are present and the verifier exposes them, but with perfect (for the verifier) generation there is no measurable repair benefit [1–6].
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment evaluating bounded GVR for intent→configuration NetOps on a public synthetic task bank. Under the executed shared-generation semantics every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier (n11 = 240), yielding a degenerate paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not add verifier-detectable value in this artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred. Two preregistration/execution deviations constrain inference: (1) generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate invalidated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption and removed discordance potential; and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed and the archived artifacts contain no recorded rationale. We release the authoritative archived artifacts (execution manifest, validator traces, and frozen analysis outputs) so others can reproduce the accounting and extend the evaluation under independent-generation, adversarial/golden-task injections, multi-model regimes, and expanded verifier coverage to more robustly assess GVR’s operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
